B11C001.summary: After the Kaurava army is destroyed, the blind king Dhritarashtra sinks into despair over the loss of his sons and allies. Sanjaya tries to console him by reminding him that grief is pointless and that he himself brought the ruin on his house through his indulgence of Duryodhana. Vidura then steps in to continue the comfort, setting up the long moral discourse that follows.

scenes.B11C001S01: Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra and the survivors did after the war, and Vaishampayana describes the king collapsing in grief while Sanjaya urges him to stop mourning.
scenes.B11C001S02: Dhritarashtra laments his losses and blames his own past faults, then Sanjaya scolds him for indulging his son and urges him to bear his grief, and Vidura speaks again.

shots.B11C001S01H02: Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Sarasvati before the story begins.
shots.B11C001S01H03: Janamejaya asks what the old king and the surviving warriors did once they heard the news of the defeat.
shots.B11C001S01H04: Vaishampayana says Dhritarashtra was stricken after losing his hundred sons, and Sanjaya told him that grief serves no purpose and that the funeral rites must now be performed.
shots.B11C001S01H05: Dhritarashtra, bereft of his sons and advisers, falls to the ground like a felled tree.
shots.B11C001S02H01: Dhritarashtra mourns his losses, says he now wishes to die, and admits he ignored the advice he was given, including Krishna's proposal for peace.
shots.B11C001S02H02: Sanjaya tries to comfort him, blaming Duryodhana's pride and the king's own favouritism, and urges him to be steady; Vidura then speaks again to the king.

B11C002.summary: Vidura tries to lift Dhritarashtra out of his grief by arguing that death comes to everyone and that the warriors who died in battle have won a noble fate. He says that mourning cannot bring the dead back and only deepens suffering. He ends by telling the king that one's own actions decide one's fate.

scenes.B11C002S01: Vidura speaks to Dhritarashtra at length, urging him to rise, accept death as the common end of all beings, and stop indulging in sorrow over the warriors slain in battle.

shots.B11C002S01H01: Vaishampayana introduces Vidura's comforting words to Dhritarashtra.
shots.B11C002S01H02: Vidura urges the king to stand up, says death takes everyone, argues that the fallen warriors have gone to a good end, and says that a life of actions bears its own fruit.

B11C003.summary: Dhritarashtra says Vidura's words have eased his grief and asks how the wise free themselves from sorrow. Vidura answers that all worldly things are impermanent and that the body is like a house that wears out, while the soul passes from one body to another like a man changing clothes. He compares the fate of creatures to pots that break at many stages of making and to swimmers who dive and surface, and he says the wise attain the highest end.

scenes.B11C003S01: Dhritarashtra thanks Vidura and asks how the wise escape sorrow, and Vidura replies with a long account of impermanence, the body as a temporary dwelling, and the role of past deeds.

shots.B11C003S01H01: Dhritarashtra says Vidura's words have dispelled his grief and asks how the wise free themselves from mental suffering.
shots.B11C003S01H02: Vidura says that the wise overcome both grief and joy, that worldly concerns are fleeting, and that the body is like a house which is eventually destroyed, while the self endures and creatures reap the fruits of their actions.

B11C004.summary: Dhritarashtra asks Vidura how the wilderness of this world can be understood, and Vidura describes the course of life from conception through birth, suffering, and death. He shows how desire, greed, and pride blind people to their own mortality. He concludes that those who practise virtue and hold to truth can cross safely over life's difficulties.

scenes.B11C004S01: Dhritarashtra asks for an explanation of the world's wilderness, and Vidura traces the stages of life from the womb through the sufferings and delusions of the living to the final death, urging virtue as the way out.

shots.B11C004S01H01: Dhritarashtra asks how the wilderness of this world can be known and asks Vidura to explain it.
shots.B11C004S01H02: Vidura describes the stages of a creature's life from conception and birth, the calamities and diseases it meets, the greed and pride that blind it, and the death that comes unnoticed, ending with the advice to practise virtue and hold to truth.

B11C005.summary: Dhritarashtra asks Vidura for a fuller account of how the wilderness of duties can be safely crossed, and Vidura tells a parable. A Brahmana is trapped in a dangerous forest, falls into a pit, hangs upside down from creepers, and is threatened from every side. He keeps sipping honey and clinging to hope even as rats gnaw at the roots of the tree he hangs from.

scenes.B11C005S01: Dhritarashtra asks for a detailed teaching, and Vidura begins a parable about a Brahmana lost in a terrifying forest, caught in a pit, dangling from creepers, and surrounded by dangers, yet still hoping to live.

shots.B11C005S01H01: Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to explain in detail the kind of understanding that lets one safely cross the wilderness of duties.
shots.B11C005S01H02: Vidura begins the parable of a Brahmana who wanders into a forest full of beasts, is hemmed in by a frightful woman and snakes, falls into a hidden pit, hangs from creepers, and is threatened by an elephant, rats, and bees while he sips honey and still clings to life.

B11C006.summary: Dhritarashtra asks how the man in the parable can be freed from his dangers and why he clings so strongly to life. Vidura explains that the parable is an allegory for human existence: the forest is the world, the pit is the body, and the dangers are disease, old age, death, desire, and the passing years. He concludes that understanding this allows a person to cut free from life's bonds.

scenes.B11C006S01: Dhritarashtra asks how the man in the parable might be rescued, and Vidura reveals that each element of the story stands for an aspect of human life, from the body and time to desire and the passing seasons.

shots.B11C006S01H01: Dhritarashtra expresses pity for the man in the parable and asks how he can be freed and where he lives.
shots.B11C006S01H02: Vidura says the parable is a figure for life: the forest is the world, the pit is the body, the beasts are diseases, the snake below is Time, the elephant is the year, the rats and snakes are days and nights, and the bees and honey are desires and their pleasures, and that knowing this lets one break free.

B11C007.summary: Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to continue, and Vidura gives a fuller teaching on escaping the cycle of rebirth. He compares the body to a chariot, the senses to horses, and the mind to the driver, and says self-control, contentment, truthfulness and harmlessness lead to liberation. He ends by saying that the wise escape the wheel of life while the foolish keep wandering in it.

scenes.B11C007S01: Dhritarashtra praises the parable and asks for more, and Vidura gives a long discourse on life as a journey, the body as a chariot, the senses as horses, and self-restraint and compassion as the way to freedom.

shots.B11C007S01H01: Dhritarashtra praises Vidura's parable and asks him to say more.
shots.B11C007S01H02: Vidura describes life as a long road and the world as a forest of diseases and dangers, uses the chariot image to explain how the senses and the mind pull a person into rebirth, and urges self-restraint, harmlessness and compassion as the way to reach the highest state.

B11C008.summary: Dhritarashtra collapses in grief and tries to end his life, but the attendants revive him. Vyasa then reminds him that all things are impermanent and that the war was fated, and he tells the story of Earth's plea to the gods, which led Vishnu to send Duryodhana to bring about the destruction of the Kauravas. Vyasa argues that the Pandavas were blameless, urges the king to live for their sake and for his own good name, and Dhritarashtra agrees to bear his grief and go on living before Vyasa leaves.

scenes.B11C008S01: Dhritarashtra faints, is revived, and wishes to die, then Vyasa explains that the war was destiny, recounts the divine origin of Duryodhana, and urges the king to live, after which Dhritarashtra accepts this and Vyasa departs.

shots.B11C008S01H01: Dhritarashtra faints after Vidura's words, is revived by his friends and attendants, and in his grief says he will end his life, until Vyasa begins to speak to him.
shots.B11C008S01H02: Vyasa tells Dhritarashtra that the king knows all things are impermanent, that the war was a fated consequence of Duryodhana's hostility, that Vidura tried hard for peace, and then recounts how Earth asked the gods for relief and Vishnu said Duryodhana would bring about the slaughter, and that the Pandavas were blameless and the king should live for their sake.
shots.B11C008S01H03: Dhritarashtra says he is overwhelmed but will not give up his life, and Vyasa vanishes.

B11C009.summary: After Vyasa leaves, Janamejaya asks what the king and the others did next, and Vaishampayana explains that Sanjaya returns with grim news: the kings and Duryodhana are dead and the rites must be performed. Dhritarashtra falls to the ground in shock, and Vidura again tries to console him, repeating that death is the common end of all creatures and that the fallen warriors have gone to heaven.

scenes.B11C009S01: Janamejaya asks what happened after Vyasa left, and Sanjaya returns and reports the deaths, prompting Dhritarashtra to collapse and Vidura to offer comfort once more.

shots.B11C009S01H01: Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra, Yudhishthira, and Kripa and the others did after Vyasa departed, and asks what Sanjaya said next.
shots.B11C009S01H02: Vaishampayana says that after Duryodhana and the army were slain, Sanjaya returned to Dhritarashtra, having lost his divine sight.
shots.B11C009S01H03: Sanjaya tells the king that the kings and his sons have all gone to death and that the funeral rites must now be performed.
shots.B11C009S01H04: Hearing this, the king falls to the ground, and Vidura tries to lift him up, repeating that death is the common end, grief cannot bring back the dead, and the fallen heroes have gone to heaven.

B11C010.summary: Dhritarashtra orders his chariot and asks for Gandhari and the royal ladies, including Kunti, to be brought to him. They gather in grief and Vidura leads them out of the city toward the battlefield. The whole city, including its children and craftsmen, is seized with mourning, and the scene is described as a second cosmic dissolution.

scenes.B11C010S01: Dhritarashtra orders the royal women to be brought out, and they come together in wailing, then Vidura escorts them from the city while the whole population of Hastinapura joins in mourning.

shots.B11C010S01H01: Dhritarashtra orders the royal ladies, Gandhari and Kunti among them, to be brought to him, and they gather and weep together while Vidura leads them out of the city toward the battlefield, with the citizens following and mourning loudly.

B11C011.summary: On the road, Dhritarashtra meets Kripa, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma, the only three of Duryodhana's great warriors still alive. They tell him that Duryodhana has died and that they themselves killed the Pandava sons and the Panchalas in their sleeping camp, then fled before the Pandavas can retaliate. Kripa urges Gandhari and the king to accept the deaths as a warrior's honour, and the three then separate, with Ashvatthama going to Vyasa's hermitage.

scenes.B11C011S01: Kripa, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma report Duryodhana's death and their night massacre of the Pandava camp, then Kripa consoles Gandhari and the king, after which the three warriors part ways.

shots.B11C011S01H01: On the road, the three surviving warriors tell the blind king of Duryodhana's death, confess their night massacre of the Pandava camp, ask leave to flee, and then part from each other, with Ashvatthama heading for Vyasa's hermitage, and the text notes that the Pandavas later meet Ashvatthama and defeat him.

B11C012.summary: Yudhishthira goes out with his brothers, Krishna and the women to meet his uncle Dhritarashtra, who has left Hastinapura in grief. The grieving women confront Yudhishthira with accusations, and the blind king embraces him without warmth. Dhritarashtra then tries to crush Bhima in his arms, but Krishna has substituted an iron figure, and the king breaks it and collapses in grief and blood.

scenes.B11C012S01: Yudhishthira meets the lamenting women and then his uncle, who embraces him reluctantly, then seeks to crush Bhima, but Krishna has put an iron image in Bhima's place and the king breaks it, falls, and is soothed and rebuked by Krishna.

shots.B11C012S01H01: Yudhishthira and the Pandavas, with Krishna, Draupadi and others, set out to meet Dhritarashtra and find the grieving women of the Kuru household, who accuse Yudhishthira of cruelty; Dhritarashtra embraces him without much warmth, then seeks Bhima, and Krishna's iron figure of Bhima is crushed by the blind king, who is left bleeding; Krishna then explains that Bhima was not hurt and urges the king to accept the peace.

B11C013.summary: Krishna, after the king has been washed, rebukes Dhritarashtra for his wrath and reminds him that his own choices and his son's bad counsel brought the ruin on him. The king admits his parental affection led him from righteousness and says he is now free of anger. He then embraces Bhima and the twin sons of Madri, and blesses them.

scenes.B11C013S01: Krishna reproaches Dhritarashtra for following Duryodhana and ignoring advice, then the king admits his wrong, sets aside his anger, and embraces the Pandava brothers.

shots.B11C013S01H01: After the king is washed, Krishna reminds him of his learning and of the warnings given before the war, blames him for letting Duryodhana rule him, and urges him to restrain his anger toward Bhima.
shots.B11C013S01H02: Dhritarashtra agrees that Krishna is right, admits parental love led him astray, says he is now free of wrath, and embraces Bhima, Arjuna and the twins, weeping and blessing them.

B11C014.summary: Gandhari, grieving for her hundred sons, wants to curse Yudhishthira, but Vyasa steps in and urges her to forgive. He reminds her that she always told Duryodhana that victory lies where righteousness is. Gandhari replies that she bears the Pandavas no ill will, blames Duryodhana and Shakuni for the ruin, and says her real anger is at Bhima's blow to Duryodhana's navel in the mace fight.

scenes.B11C014S01: The Pandavas go to see Gandhari, Vyasa arrives to head off her curse, and he reminds her of her own words of righteousness, and Gandhari responds that her grief is real but she is angered by Bhima's foul blow to Duryodhana.

shots.B11C014S01H01: The Pandavas visit Gandhari, who wishes to curse Yudhishthira, so Vyasa arrives and tells her to forgive, reminding her that she always said victory lies with righteousness, and Gandhari replies that she wishes no harm to the Pandavas, blames her own sons and Karna, and objects to Bhima striking Duryodhana below the navel.

B11C015.summary: Bhima defends his conduct in the battle as a response to Duryodhana's injustices and to his own vow, and Gandhari scolds him for drinking Duhshasana's blood. Gandhari then rages at the Pandavas for the death of her sons, and Yudhishthira offers himself to her curse. She withholds it, and her gaze injures his toe, after which she comforts the Pandavas. The chapter closes with the reunion of Kunti and Draupadi and the grief of the women, and the section is marked as ending.

scenes.B11C015S01: Bhima defends his deeds to Gandhari, who rebukes him and then grieves, while Yudhishthira offers himself to her curse, she comforts the Pandavas, and the women lament together before the closing line of the section.

shots.B11C015S01H01: Frightened, Bhima defends his foul acts as done out of fear and self-defence, citing Duryodhana's treachery, the insult to Draupadi and the years of exile; Gandhari rebukes him for drinking Duhshasana's blood, and Bhima replies that he only smeared his hands and was bound by his vow.
shots.B11C015S01H02: Gandhari laments that Bhima did not spare even one of her sons, leaving the blind couple without any support in their old age, though she would have grieved less had he kept to righteousness.
shots.B11C015S01H03: Gandhari asks where Yudhishthira is, and he presents himself to her curse; she says nothing, and her glance through the cloth over her eyes injures his toe. She then comforts the Pandavas, and Kunti embraces her sons and weeps with Draupadi.
shots.B11C015S01H04: Draupadi laments the loss of her children, and Kunti comforts her before they go to Gandhari together, and Gandhari answers that the destruction was caused by Time and was inevitable, so no one should grieve for it.
shots.B11C015S01H05: Closing line: the Jalapradanika parva of the Stri parva ends here.

B11C016.summary: Gandhari, though far from the battlefield, sees its carnage through her spiritual sight and begins to lament. Dhritarashtra, the Pandavas, Krishna and the Kuru women travel to Kurukshetra, where the women find their dead husbands, sons and brothers torn by beasts and birds. Gandhari, speaking to Krishna, describes the horror of the field, and her lament ends as her eyes fall on her son Duryodhana.

scenes.B11C016S01: The lamentation of the women begins with Gandhari's spiritual vision of the battlefield, the royal party's journey to Kurukshetra, the women's horror at the corpses, and Gandhari's speech to Krishna, which ends as she sees Duryodhana.

shots.B11C016S01H02: Gandhari sees the slaughter from afar with her spiritual eye, the king, the Pandavas, Krishna and the Kuru women go to the field, the women collapse at the sight of the bodies and the scavengers, Gandhari describes the carnage to Krishna, and her eyes fall on Duryodhana.

B11C017.summary: Gandhari falls senseless at the sight of Duryodhana's body and then mourns over him, recalling how she had told him that victory lies with righteousness. She says her grief is for the blind king and for the reversal of Duryodhana's fortunes, and she describes the ruin of the women and the once-glorious prince. She ends by saying he has at least won the regions of heroes.

scenes.B11C017S01: Gandhari collapses over her son's body, recalls their last exchange before the battle, mourns the fall of a once-powerful king and his grieving wife, and declares that her son has won heroes' heaven.

shots.B11C017S01H01: Gandhari faints when she sees Duryodhana lying dead, then revives, embraces him and mourns, recalling her words before the battle and her grief for the blind king, while describing the fallen prince, the mourning of his wife, and his reversal of fortune, before concluding that he has attained the heroes' regions.

B11C018.summary: Gandhari moves on to lament the other sons she has lost, and she grieves most for the young widows wandering on the battlefield. She describes the ruin of the royal household and the shame of women now exposed to common eyes. She singles out Duhshasana, whose insult to Draupadi and whose death at Bhima's hands she recounts, and she recalls her unheeded warnings to Duryodhana to make peace.

scenes.B11C018S01: Gandhari recounts the deaths of her sons, the suffering of the daughters-in-law, and the fall of Duhshasana, reminding Krishna of the insult to Draupadi and of her own failed warnings to Duryodhana.

shots.B11C018S01H01: Gandhari grieves for her hundred sons slain by Bhima, for the young widows wandering among the dead, and for the shame of the royal women, then recalls Duhshasana's insult to Draupadi, her own warnings to Duryodhana to cast off Shakuni and make peace, and Bhima's drinking of Duhshasana's blood.

B11C019.summary: Gandhari continues her lament by naming her dead sons one after another, Vikarna, Durmukha, Citrasena, Vivingsati and Duhsaha. For each she describes the body, the wounds, the scavenging birds and beasts, and the grieving women around him. The chapter stresses the beauty and promise of the young men lost in the war.

scenes.B11C019S01: Gandhari mourns her sons Vikarna, Durmukha, Citrasena, Vivingsati and Duhsaha in turn, describing each body and the grief of the women who remain with them.

shots.B11C019S01H01: Gandhari names her sons Vikarna, Durmukha, Citrasena, Vivingsati and Duhsaha one by one, describing each slain body, the wounds, the birds and beasts gathered there, and the grieving wives and women around them.

B11C020.summary: Gandhari continues her lament by mourning Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, and imagines the grief of his young wife Uttara, daughter of Virata, as she mourns him and speaks to him. The Matsya ladies then drag Uttara away from the body of her slain father Virata, and Gandhari lists other fallen young men. The chapter shows the war's cost falling on the young and on the women left behind.

scenes.B11C020S01: Gandhari mourns Abhimanyu and describes his widow Uttara weeping over him and addressing him, then the Matsya women drag Uttara from the body of her father Virata, and Gandhari names other young men slain in the battle.

shots.B11C020S01H01: Gandhari praises Abhimanyu's courage and describes Uttara, the daughter of Virata, weeping over her dead husband, speaking to him and blaming the warriors who killed him, before the Matsya women drag Uttara away from the body of her father Virata and Gandhari names other fallen youths.

B11C021.summary: Gandhari mourns Karna, who was slain by Arjuna after he had killed many great warriors. She describes his wives and the mother of his son Vrishasena weeping over him, and Karna's widow blames the curse of his teacher and Arjuna's arrow for his death. She notes that Yudhishthira could not sleep for thirteen years because of his fear of Karna.

scenes.B11C021S01: Gandhari mourns Karna's death at Arjuna's hands, describes his wives lamenting and his mother-in-law faint at the sight, and notes the animals that have already started feeding on his corpse.

shots.B11C021S01H01: Gandhari mourns Karna, once a fierce fire, now slain by Arjuna and lying on the ground, with his women weeping, Yudhishthira's long sleeplessness, and the wives blaming the curse and the arrow that ended him, while the body is being torn by scavengers.

B11C022.summary: Gandhari mourns several fallen men who had once been powerful: the lord of Avanti slain by Bhima, Bahlika, and Jayadratha, who was killed by Arjuna. She tells how Jayadratha's wives guard his body and how her widowed daughter Duhshala runs about searching for her husband's head. She recalls the old wrong done to Draupadi and the sparing of Jayadratha out of regard for Duhshala.

scenes.B11C022S01: Gandhari points out the bodies of the lord of Avanti, Bahlika and Jayadratha, speaks of Jayadratha's widows and her daughter Duhshala, and remembers how Jayadratha once tried to dishonour Draupadi.

shots.B11C022S01H01: Gandhari mourns the lord of Avanti, Bahlika and Jayadratha as they lie among scavengers, describes Jayadratha's wives guarding his body, recalls how he was spared earlier out of regard for Duhshala, and grieves that her daughter is now a widow searching for her husband's head.

B11C023.summary: Gandhari lists the great warriors who have fallen. She mourns Shalya, slain by Yudhishthira, and Bhagadatta, and then speaks of Bhishma lying on a bed of arrows, whose death she sees as the fall of a sun among men. She laments Drona, whose body is burned on a pyre attended by his wife Kripi and his disciples, who then carry her toward the Ganga.

scenes.B11C023S01: Gandhari mourns in turn Shalya, Bhagadatta, Bhishma on his bed of arrows, and Drona, whose funeral pyre is lit and attended by his wife Kripi and disciples as they head for the Ganga.

shots.B11C023S01H01: Gandhari mourns Shalya, Bhagadatta, Bhishma on his arrow bed, and Drona, describing their bodies, their great deeds and the grief of their women, then tells how Drona's disciples light his pyre while Kripi grieves, and how they go on toward the Ganga.

B11C024.summary: Gandhari describes the death of Bhurishrava, whose arm was cut off by Arjuna and who was then killed by Satyaki while sitting in a vow. His widows weep over his severed arm, and Gandhari's speech of rebuke to Krishna is given through the widows. She ends by mourning Shakuni, slain by Sahadeva, and fears that he will sow discord among her sons in the next world.

scenes.B11C024S01: Gandhari describes Somadatta mourning his son Bhurishrava, whose widows hold his severed arm and rebuke Arjuna and Satyaki, and then she turns to the death of Shakuni at Sahadeva's hand and her fear that he will stir up trouble in the next world.

shots.B11C024S01H01: Gandhari describes Somadatta grieving over his son, and Bhurishrava's widows lying on the ground with his severed arm in their laps, and blaming Arjuna for the arm and Satyaki for killing Bhurishrava while he sat in a vow.
shots.B11C024S01H02: The widows speak over the arm, recalling the strength of the hand that once held many women and fought many foes, and they reproach Arjuna for striking it off, until the chief lady falls silent and the co-wives weep with her.
shots.B11C024S01H03: Gandhari mourns Shakuni, slain by Sahadeva and now being fanned by birds, recalls his deceit at dice that won Yudhishthira's kingdom, and fears that his trickery might divide her sons in the next world.

B11C025.summary: Gandhari continues her lament over the fallen kings and warriors, from the Kambojas and Magadhas to Drupada, Dhrishtaketu and Vinda and Anuvinda. She then blames Krishna for standing aside while the Kurus destroyed each other, and she curses him that within thirty-six years he will lose his own kin and die in the wilderness. Krishna accepts the curse with a faint smile, saying that the Yadavas will fall by each other's hands, and the Pandavas are left stunned.

scenes.B11C025S01: Gandhari mourns a long list of fallen kings and their women, then faints, blames Krishna for not preventing the war, and curses him; Krishna replies that the Yadavas will perish by their own hands, and the Pandavas despair.

shots.B11C025S01H01: Gandhari mourns the Kamboja ruler and his queen, the Kalinga and Magadha rulers, Brihadbala of Kosala, the sons of Dhrishtadyumna, the Kekaya brothers, Drupada, Dhrishtaketu and his son, Lakshmana, and Vinda and Anuvinda, and she says Krishna and the Pandavas have escaped many great warriors while her sons did not, then complains that Krishna did nothing to stop the war.
shots.B11C025S01H02: Gandhari swoons with grief and anger and places all the blame for the war on Krishna.
shots.B11C025S01H03: Gandhari accuses Krishna of standing aside from the slaughter despite his power to stop it, and curses him to kill his own kin, to die in the wilderness thirty-six years later, and to see his women mourn as the Kuru women do.
shots.B11C025S01H04: Krishna calmly replies that only he can destroy the Vrishnis, that the curse helps him do this, and that the Yadavas will be killed by one another, and the Pandavas are left stunned and despairing.

B11C026.summary: A holy figure, identified only as the holy one, tells Gandhari that her son Duryodhana's wicked character brought the carnage and that grief only multiplies grief. Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira how many fell and where the warriors have gone, and Yudhishthira tells him the tally and the destinations of the dead, which depend on how they died. Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira knows this, and he credits a boon of spiritual vision from the sage Lomasa; Dhritarashtra then asks how the bodies should be honoured, and Yudhishthira orders the funeral rites performed for all the dead. The burning of the dead is described in detail before the Pandavas lead Dhritarashtra toward the Ganga.

scenes.B11C026S01: The holy one rebukes Gandhari, Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira for the tally of the fallen and their fates, and Yudhishthira describes the regions where the warriors went according to how they died.
scenes.B11C026S02: Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira has such knowledge, and Yudhishthira explains that he got spiritual sight from Lomasa, then Dhritarashtra asks about the rites, and Yudhishthira has the dead of both sides cremated before going to the Ganga.

shots.B11C026S01H01: The holy one tells Gandhari to stop grieving, says that Duryodhana's arrogance and cruelty caused the carnage, that grief only doubles itself, and he contrasts the purposes for which women of different classes bear children with the fate of a princess's sons, who are born to be slain.
shots.B11C026S01H02: Gandhari stays silent, and Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira how many fell and how many survived.
shots.B11C026S01H03: Yudhishthira gives the tally of the fallen and of the survivors.
shots.B11C026S01H04: Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira what destinations the warriors have reached.
shots.B11C026S01H05: Yudhishthira says warriors who fell bravely go to Indra's realm, those who died without courage go to the Gandharvas, those who fled or begged for mercy go to the Guhyakas, those who fell fighting unarmed go to Brahman, and the rest go to the Uttara Kurus.
shots.B11C026S02H01: Dhritarashtra asks by what knowledge Yudhishthira sees these things as if he were an ascetic with perfect insight.
shots.B11C026S02H02: Yudhishthira says that during his forest wanderings on pilgrimage he received spiritual sight from the sage Lomasa.
shots.B11C026S02H03: Dhritarashtra asks who will perform the last rites for the friendless dead and for those whose bodies lie unburied and torn by birds.
shots.B11C026S02H04: Yudhishthira orders Sudharma, Dhaumya, Sanjaya, Vidura, Yuyutsu and others to ensure the dead are cremated; they build pyres, burn the kings in order, including Duryodhana and his brothers and many other heroes, burn the friendless dead together, and then Yudhishthira leads Dhritarashtra to the Ganga.

B11C027.summary: At the Ganga, the Kuru women give water offerings to their dead, and Kunti reveals that Karna was her eldest son by the sun god, born before her marriage. The Pandavas grieve, and Yudhishthira laments that the secret was kept and that the war could have been avoided. He makes water offerings to Karna and to his widows and kin, and the section ends with the colophon of the Stri Parva and the Mahabharata's author.

scenes.B11C027S01: At the Ganga the women make water offerings, Kunti tells her sons that Karna was their brother, Yudhishthira laments and makes the offering for Karna, and then the Stri Parva closes with its colophon.

shots.B11C027S01H01: At the Ganga, the Kuru women cast off their ornaments and offer water to their dead; Kunti reveals that Karna was her son by Surya and the Pandavas' eldest brother, and Yudhishthira laments the concealment and the grief it brought, makes the water offering for Karna, and rises from the river.
shots.B11C027S01H02: Closing line: the Stri Parva ends.
shots.B11C027S01H03: Colophon: the title of the Mahabharata.
